At $k_{\rm leg}=15\ \mathrm{kN/m}$, $v_x=4.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$ and $|v_y|=0.7\ \mathrm{m/s}$ the asymmetry $v_y^{\rm to}-|v_y^{\rm td}|$ runs from $+1.37\ \mathrm{m/s}$ at $\alpha_0=58^\circ$ to $-1.47\ \mathrm{m/s}$ at $80^\circ$, crossing zero at $\alpha_0=68.2^\circ$; that stride has $t_{\rm c}=0.192\ \mathrm s$, $t_{\rm f}=0.143\ \mathrm s$ and duty factor $\beta=0.29$, comfortably inside the running regime of Proposition 1.2. This recovers a control input ($\alpha_0$) from a desired output (periodicity), which no forward formula gives.
K3. Given a measured vertical GRF trace $F(t)$ over one push-off, recover the takeoff velocity and jump height by numerical integration, then propagate a $\pm5\%$ uncertainty in body mass into the height estimate. Probes: Lab 2; inverse + sensitivity.
Solution
Trapezoidally integrate the net impulse $\int(F-mg)\,dt$, divide by $m$ for $v_0$, then $h=v_0^2/2g$. For sensitivity, at a fixed measured force trace $mg$ scales with $m$, so the net impulse and $v_0$ shift with mass; because $v_0=(\int F\,dt)/m-g\,t_{\rm p}$ carries the mass in the denominator and $h\propto v_0^2$, the height error is amplified and opposite in sign - $\tfrac{\delta h/h}{\delta m/m}=-2\big(1+g\,t_{\rm p}/v_0\big)=-4.42$ for Lab 2's push-off ($t_{\rm p}=0.30\ \mathrm s$, $v_0=2.43\ \mathrm{m/s}$) - so a $+5\%$ mass error shifts the estimated height from $30.04$ to $24.04\ \mathrm{cm}$, a $-20.0\%$ change. The exercise is measurement inversion plus error propagation, not evaluation.
K4. Subject to a fixed peak force and push-off distance, optimise the shape of the push-off force profile to maximise jump height. Probes: Lab 2; constrained optimization.
Solution
Parametrise the profile by how front-loaded it is, compute the height from each profile's net impulse, and search for the maximum under the fixed peak-force ceiling. The sweep gives $h=25.95,\ 30.04,\ 32.05,\ 32.38,\ 30.04,\ 20.02\ \mathrm{cm}$ at front-loading $1.3,\ 1.0,\ 0.8,\ 0.7,\ 0.5,\ 0.3$: an interior maximum at $0.7$, worth $32.4\ \mathrm{cm}$ against the symmetric $30.0$. The optimum is a property of the model, not of muscle. Front-loading helps at first because reaching the ceiling earlier fills more area under the force-time curve at the same peak. Past $0.7$ the same shape parameter also narrows the pulse, and the area lost off the end of the push-off outgrows the area gained at the start; the two effects balance at $0.7$. A real jumper meets a second, tighter limit that this profile family does not model - force cannot rise infinitely fast - so the physiological optimum sits at less front-loading than $0.7$, and the gap between the two is the honest measure of what the impulse argument alone can claim.
K5. Compare countermovement and squat jumps across a range of front-loading at fixed peak force, and quantify the impulse gain and its height payoff. Probes: Lab 2; regime comparison.
Solution
Sweep the front-loading parameter, computing net impulse and height for each; plot both regimes. The front-loaded (countermovement) profile carries a larger impulse for the same peak, and because $h\propto v_0^2\propto(\text{impulse})^2$ the height gain is amplified relative to the impulse gain: net impulse $169.9\to175.5\ \mathrm{N\,s}$ is $+3.3\%$, and height $30.04\to32.05\ \mathrm{cm}$ is $+6.7\%$, twice as much, as the square demands. The comparison isolates how much of the real countermovement advantage the impulse mechanism alone explains, leaving the rest to elastic and reflex contributions.
K6. For a range of drop heights $h_{\rm drop}$, find the minimum stopping distance $d_{\rm s}$ that keeps the average landing force below a tissue-tolerance threshold. Probes: Lab 3; inverse / design.
Solution
Invert $\bar F=\tfrac12 m v_{\rm land}^2/d_{\rm s}+mg\le F_{\rm tol}$ for $d_{\rm s}$: $d_{\rm s}\ge\tfrac12 m v_{\rm land}^2/(F_{\rm tol}-mg)$, with $v_{\rm land}=\sqrt{2gh_{\rm drop}}$. Substituting $v_{\rm land}^2=2gh_{\rm drop}$ collapses the whole expression to $d_{\rm s}\ge mgh_{\rm drop}/(F_{\rm tol}-mg)$, exactly linear in drop height with every other quantity in the constant. Taking $F_{\rm tol}=6mg$ as the assumed tolerance, the constant is $\tfrac15$: the required give is $4,\ 8,\ 12,\ 16$ and $20\ \mathrm{cm}$ for drops of $0.2,\ 0.4,\ 0.6,\ 0.8$ and $1.0\ \mathrm m$. So a landing that is safe from a low box demands a proportionately deeper flex from a high one, and the deepest squat a person can control - roughly $40\ \mathrm{cm}$ of centre-of-mass travel - caps the drop at about $2\ \mathrm m$ at this tolerance. This is a design inversion: solving for the give a safe landing needs, then reading off the height at which the give runs out.
K7. Sweep the tendon resilience $R$ and compute the muscle's mechanical work per step; find where the economy degrades fastest. Probes: Lab 4; sensitivity.
Solution
Compute $W_{\rm musc}=(1-R)U$ and the economy factor $2/(1-R)$ across $R$. The factor rises hyperbolically, and its sensitivity $d/dR[2/(1-R)]=2/(1-R)^2$ diverges as $R\to1$, so near the healthy $R\approx0.92$ a small loss of resilience already costs a large fractional rise in muscular work. Numerically: at $R=0.92$ the economy factor is $25.0$ and the sensitivity $2/(1-R)^2=312.5$; at $R=0.80$ they are $10.0$ and $50.0$, a sensitivity six times smaller. Dropping resilience by four points, $0.92\to0.88$, raises the muscle's work per step from $2.48$ to $3.72\ \mathrm J$ - fifty percent more work for a four-percent worse spring. This is why a modest decline in tendon quality has an outsized metabolic penalty - a nonlinearity, not a number to plug in.
K8. Model the impact transient as a mass on a contact spring and sweep the contact stiffness; find the stiffness that keeps the loading rate below an injury threshold. Probes: section 9; inverse.
Solution
With loading rate $\approx\tfrac{2}{\pi}v_{\rm imp}k_{\rm c}$, invert for the largest admissible $k_{\rm c}=\tfrac{\pi}{2}(\text{rate}_{\rm tol})/v_{\rm imp}$, and check the resulting peak $v_{\rm imp}\sqrt{k_{\rm c}m_{\rm imp}}$. Because the rate scales linearly with $k_{\rm c}$ but the peak only as $\sqrt{k_{\rm c}}$, softening the contact buys a large reduction in loading rate for a smaller reduction in peak: halving $k_{\rm c}$ halves the rate but cuts the peak by only $1-1/\sqrt2=29\%$. With the §9 values $m_{\rm imp}=8\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $v_{\rm imp}=1.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$, a tolerance of $100$ body weights per second admits $k_{\rm c}\le107.9\ \mathrm{kN/m}$, where the peak is $1.35$ body weights - against $1.84$ body weights and $185$ per second on the $200\ \mathrm{kN/m}$ concrete. Cushioning bought a $46\%$ cut in rate for a $27\%$ cut in peak, which is why cushioning is specified against the rate.
K9. Using a fatigue law and a damage-accumulation rule, compute the number of loading cycles to a bone stress fracture at a given per-step stress, and find the weekly mileage that reaches the fatigue limit. Probes: section 9; simulation + inverse.
Solution
Take a fatigue curve $N(\sigma)$ (cycles to failure falling steeply with per-step stress $\sigma$) and accumulate damage by Miner's rule, $D=\sum n_i/N_i$; failure at $D=1$. For a per-step stress and a weekly step count, solve for the mileage at which accumulated cycles reach $N(\sigma)$ within the bone's repair window. Assume a Basquin-type curve $N(\sigma)=N_0(\sigma_0/\sigma)^{1/b}$ with $N_0=10^4$ cycles at $\sigma_0=60\ \mathrm{MPa}$ measured, not derived: the fatigue-strength coefficient of a Basquin curve is fitted to cyclic-loading tests on bone specimens, not computed from this course's chemistry or mechanics. The pair $(N_0,\sigma_0)$ is one fitted point on that curve, not two independent measurements - $N_0=10^4$ carries the same provenance. and exponent $b=0.12$ (assumed; the exponent is what a real study would measure), and $700$ loading cycles per kilometre for one limb. At a per-step stress of $45\ \mathrm{MPa}$ that gives $N=1.10\times10^5$ cycles, or $157\ \mathrm{km}$ - about $39\ \mathrm{km}$ per week if the damage must not close within four weeks. Raise the per-step stress to $50\ \mathrm{MPa}$, an eleven percent change, and $N$ falls to $4.6\times10^4$: $65\ \mathrm{km}$, or $16\ \mathrm{km}$ per week. An eleven percent stiffer stride costs a factor $2.4$ in safe mileage. That steepness is the whole point: the dose, not one bad step, is what fractures the bone, and the dose depends violently on a quantity a runner changes without noticing.
K10. Build simple metabolic-cost models for walking and running as functions of speed, and locate the crossover speed at which running becomes cheaper. Probes: section 4; regime comparison.
Solution
Model walking cost as rising steeply with speed (pendular collision losses growing as the vault is pushed toward its $\mathrm{Fr}=1$ limit) and running cost as flatter (elastic return capping the per-distance work); plot both against speed. Their intersection is the crossover. Where it lands is set entirely by the two curves' free parameters, and that is the point of the problem: with one plausible pair - walking cost $\propto\mathrm{Fr}^2/(1-0.85\,\mathrm{Fr})$, running cost near-flat - the crossover falls at $v=2.6\ \mathrm{m/s}$, i.e. $\mathrm{Fr}=0.71$, and small changes to either curve move it. So the observed $\mathrm{Fr}\approx\tfrac12$ is not a prediction of this model; it is the number the model must be calibrated to, and calibrating it is what fixes the otherwise free running-cost offset. What the exercise does deliver without calibration is the qualitative structure and one hard bound: two competing regimes produce a crossover at all, and it must lie below the kinematic ceiling $\mathrm{Fr}=1$ of (4.2), because past that ceiling walking is not available at any cost. Keeping the derived ceiling and the fitted transition apart is the same discipline §4 applies.
K11. Section 7's three-system model was built top-down: a measured maximal oxygen uptake and a measured energy equivalent of oxygen gave a structural critical power $CP\approx1829\ \mathrm W$. Now go bottom-up: treat six world running records as a power–duration dataset, fit Proposition 7.2's hyperbola $P=CP+W'/t$ to them by inverse regression, check how sensitive that fit is to which records are used, and see whether the two routes land in the same place. Probes: section 7 Proposition 7.2; inverse fit + sensitivity + regime comparison.

Six world-record performances (800 m to marathon) converted to a metabolic power via the running-cost constant $\mathrm{CoT}_{\rm run}$ defined in this solution (distinct from Module 8's speed-dependent walking $\mathrm{CoT}(v)$), and Proposition 7.2's hyperbola fitted to them by linear regression of $P$ against $1/t$.

Solution

Take the net cost of running as roughly speed-independent over the aerobic-to-anaerobic range actually run, $\mathrm{CoT}_{\rm run}\approx4.18\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$ measured, not derived: the near-constant net metabolic cost of running per unit distance (about $1\ \mathrm{kcal\,kg^{-1}\,km^{-1}}$, the long-standing Margaria figure) is an indirect-calorimetry result, distinct from Module 8's speed-dependent walking $\mathrm{CoT}(v)$, and not a quantity this course's chemistry derives.. For each world record, $v=$ distance/time and $P=\mathrm{CoT}_{\rm run}\,v\,m$ turns a race time into a metabolic power; regressing $P$ against $1/t$ over the six points recovers $CP$ (the intercept) and $W'$ (the slope) by Proposition 7.2.

import numpy as np

CoT_run = 4.184          # J/(kg m), net cost of running, ~speed-independent
m = 70.0                 # kg, reference runner

# world-record distance (m) and time (s); approximate, published tables
records = {
    "800 m": (800.0, 100.91),
    "1500 m": (1500.0, 206.00),
    "5000 m": (5000.0, 755.36),
    "10000 m": (10000.0, 1571.00),
    "half marathon": (21097.5, 3451.0),
    "marathon": (42195.0, 7235.0),
}

t = np.array([tt for _, tt in records.values()])
speed = np.array([d / tt for d, tt in records.values()])
power = CoT_run * speed * m          # metabolic power, watts


def fit_cp_wprime(t_pts, p_pts):
    """Linear regression P = CP + W'/t, returns (CP, W')."""
    x = 1.0 / t_pts
    a_mat = np.vstack([np.ones_like(x), x]).T
    (cp, wprime), *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(a_mat, p_pts, rcond=None)
    return cp, wprime


cp_fit, wprime_fit = fit_cp_wprime(t, power)

for name, p in zip(records, power):
    print(f"{name:14s} P = {p:7.1f} W")
print(f"fit: CP = {cp_fit:.1f} W, W' = {wprime_fit / 1000:.2f} kJ")

# leave-one-out: how much does dropping one record move the fit?
cp_loo = []
for i in range(len(t)):
    mask = np.arange(len(t)) != i
    cp_i, _ = fit_cp_wprime(t[mask], power[mask])
    cp_loo.append(cp_i)
print(f"leave-one-out CP range: {min(cp_loo):.1f}-{max(cp_loo):.1f} W")

vo2max = 75.0 * m / 1000.0 / 60.0     # L/s, elite distance runner
e_o2 = 20.9e3                          # J/L, energy equivalent of O2
p_ox = vo2max * e_o2                   # metabolic oxidative ceiling, W
print(f"structural CP (VO2max=75) = {p_ox:.1f} W")

# what VO2max would the fitted CP itself imply?
vo2_implied = cp_fit / e_o2 * 1000.0 * 60.0 / m
print(f"VO2max implied by the fit = {vo2_implied:.1f} mL/kg/min")

p_marathon = power[list(records).index("marathon")]
print(f"marathon P / CP(fit) = {p_marathon / cp_fit:.3f}")
print(f"800 m P / CP(fit) = {power[0] / cp_fit:.3f}")

Output: metabolic power falls from $2321.9\ \mathrm W$ at $800\ \mathrm m$ to $1708.1\ \mathrm W$ at the marathon; the fit gives $CP=1796.9\ \mathrm W$, $W'=56.84\ \mathrm{kJ}$. Leaving out any one record moves $CP$ only to $1774$–$1832\ \mathrm W$ (the ceiling is well constrained by all six points together), but moves $W'$ from $52.1$ to $77.9\ \mathrm{kJ}$ - dropping the shortest, most anaerobic event ($800\ \mathrm m$) changes $W'$ the most, because $W'$ is set by how far short events sit above $CP$, and this six-record set has only one event that short. Read the other way, the fitted $CP$ implies a $\dot V\mathrm O_{2\max}$ of $73.7\ \mathrm{mL\,kg^{-1}\,min^{-1}}$ - a physiologically ordinary value for an elite distance runner (the $70$–$85$ range used in §7) - rather than a suspiciously exact match to the assumed $75$: the two routes agree at the level the underlying physiology allows, not to a spurious extra digit. The regime split is exactly what (7.2) predicts: the marathon sits at $95.1\%$ of the fitted $CP$, an almost entirely aerobic effort, while $800\ \mathrm m$ demands $129.2\%$ of it, a power that can only be met by drawing down $W'$, which is why that race is run to near-exhaustion of the phosphocreatine and glycolytic stores rather than of oxygen supply. The fitted $W'=56.8\ \mathrm{kJ}$ also sits just below the $63$–$125\ \mathrm{kJ}$ published range for the maximal accumulated oxygen deficit - consistent, given that the six records span only $800\ \mathrm m$ to the marathon and exclude the shorter, more purely anaerobic events (100–400–m) that best pin down the full store.

What this problem shows that neither route shows alone: the top-down structural model (built from a lung's oxygen uptake) and the bottom-up empirical fit (built from six stopwatch times) are two independent measurements of the same physiological ceiling, and a $CP$ built from one is recovered by the other to within a few per cent - well inside the spread of measured elite $\dot V\mathrm O_{2\max}$ values itself. That is the payoff of an interwoven course - a chemical quantity and a competition record checking each other, and the leave-one-out sweep showing precisely which of the two fitted numbers ($CP$, not $W'$) that check is actually trustworthy for.

What the model captures, and what it misses

The spring-loaded inverted pendulum earns its reach by discarding almost everything. Each debt is named below, and each is repaid - here or in a later module.

IdealisationWhat it dropsWhere it is repaid
Massless legswing-leg inertia and the touchdown collisionthe impact transient of section 9; whole-body coordination in Module 12
Linear, lossless springtendon nonlinearity, damping, and the muscular work that replaces lossesthe stretch-shortening economy of section 7
Point masssegments, joints, and internal angular momentuminverse dynamics and multi-segment control, Modules 12 and 15
Sagittal plane onlylateral balance, cutting, and turningperturbed running and balance, Module 10
Fixed $k_{\rm leg}$, no controlactive tuning of leg stiffness and angle of attack step to stepsensorimotor control, Modules 10 and 13

What survives is the physics the idealisations were chosen to keep: running is a bounce, a jump and a landing are one impulse read two ways, and injury is a rate and a dose against a tolerance. The idealised spring is enough to make each of these quantitative.

Repayment ledger

Module 9 discharged four debts and opens several more. It repaid Module 6 (the tendon spring becomes the whole-leg spring of running economy), Module 8 (the walk-to-run transition it handed forward is located here, and its cost-of-transport ceiling is repaid in §7), Module 2 (the deferred dynamic impact wave becomes the loading transient), and Module 0 (§7's three-system model turns a measured oxygen uptake and the ATP free energy of Module 0 §3 into the critical power that K11 then recovers independently from six world records). It forwards:

ToOwed
Module 10perturbed running and landing - slips, cuts, unexpected surfaces - and the reactive balance that a fixed-gait SLIP cannot show.
Module 12whole-body coordination and optimal control of jumping and sprinting; redundancy in multi-joint push-off.
Module 13uphill and downhill running, sprint acceleration, and sport-specific tasks beyond steady bouncing.
Module 14how tissue tolerance and repair change with age and health - tendinopathy, stress fracture, and ACL risk.
Module 15measuring these quantities: force plates, loading-rate estimation, and the impact-quantification pipeline.

This closes Module 9. Running turned Module 8's stiff-legged vault into a spring-mass bounce; the same impulse that launches a jump, read backward, tames a landing; and the tendon that Module 6 built as a spring turns out to do most of the work of running. What is left is to perturb it (Module 10), coordinate it (Module 12), vary its terrain (Module 13), age its tissues (Module 14), and measure it (Module 15).
